text: . Heart transplantation. Marked improvements have been seen in the outcome of heart transplantation since the introduction of ciclosporin, which has resulted in a re- duced incidence and severity of rejection episodes.1 The 1- year survival rate is about 80%.1,2 A common immunosuppressive regimen consists of tri- ple therapy with ciclosporin or tacrolimus, azathioprine or mycophenolate, and corticosteroids.3-6 Some centres also use induction therapy with antilymphocyte immunoglobu- lins (polyclonal antibodies) or muromonab-CD3.4,7 Induction therapy increases the risk of infection and lym- phoproliferative disorders, but does delay the first rejec- tion episode and allows transplantation in higher risk groups. It also enables calcineurin inhibitor use to be de- layed in patients with initial poor renal function7 and cor- ticosteroids to be stopped as maintenance therapy in some groups of patients.8 Muromonab-CD3 may be associated with a higher incidence of adverse reactions than polyclo- nal antibodies. Sensitisation to muromonab-CD3 is strongly associated with vascular rejection, and this and the dose-related propensity for lymphoproliferative dis- ease with muromonab-CD3 have led to a decline in its use; some consider it should be abandoned in favour of poly- clonal preparations.7,9 The interleukin-2 receptor antibod- ies basiliximab and daclizumab have also been used for induction therapy.2,7,10,11 However, daclizumab use has been associated with an increased risk of death due to in- fection, mostly in patients given additional immunosup- pressive treatment with antilymphocyte drugs for early postoperative complications.11 The interleukin-2 receptor antibodies have not as yet been associated with an addi- tional risk of malignancies.7 Alemtuzumab is under inves- tigation for induction therapy in heart transplantation.7,9 There does not seem to be any great clinical benefit of tac- rolimus over ciclosporin in heart transplant patients,9,12,13 although some have reported reduced rates of histological rejection,14,15 and there is evidence that patients of Afro- Caribbean origin in particular may be more prone to acute rejection with ciclosporin than with tacrolimus.16 It has been suggested that tacrolimus be substituted for ciclosporin in those patients suffering persistent rejection, or adverse effects associated with ciclosporin,17 or with hyperlipidaemia or hypertension.18 Microemulsifying ciclosporin may be associated with less rejection than the oil-based formulation.19 The use of mycophenolate mofetil instead of azathioprine in triple therapy has been shown to reduce mortality and rejection in the first year after heart transplantation,20 and a retrospective review21 concluded that the advent of myc- op
